'''Munakata Shrine''' (Munakata-jinja) is a Shinto shrine located within the Kyoto Imperial Garden in Kamigyō Ward, Kyoto City, Kyoto Prefecture. It is a shrine listed in the national histories, and its former shrine rank was prefectural shrine.
== Enshrined deities ==
The shrine principally enshrines the '''Three Munakata Goddesses''' (Tagorihime-no-Mikoto, Tagitsuhime-no-Mikoto, and Ichikishimahime-no-Mikoto), with Inari-no-Kami (Ukanomitama-no-Kami) and '''Ama-no-Iwato-Ake-no-Kami''' additionally enshrined.
The principal deities are recorded in the ''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku'' as being the “same deities,” although enshrined at a different location, as the Munakata Shrine of Chikuzen Province (present-day Munakata Taisha), and are also described as “the same deities at a separate shrine.” The subsidiary deity Ama-no-Iwato-Ake-no-Kami was likewise incorporated from a shrine listed in the national histories (Ame-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami). The ''Kazan’in Family Chronicle'' (quoted in the ''Yamashiro Meishōshi'') records its state before enshrinement as: “Ame-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami. A great stone. Possessing spiritual power.” Ukanomitama-no-Kami is said to have been enshrined together by Fujiwara no Tokihira.
As the shrine is currently located in the southwestern part of the Imperial Garden (the “rear demon gate”), it has attracted faith as a protector against misfortune.
== History ==
According to shrine tradition, in Enryaku 14 (795), Fujiwara no Fuyutsugu, acting on an imperial command from Emperor Kanmu, invited the Munakata deity of Chikuzen as a guardian deity of the imperial residence and enshrined it at the southwestern corner of his own residence, the Tōkyō Residence (also called the Tōkyō Ichijō Residence). As the oldest source recording the origin of the shrine’s location, the ''Tsuchiyuki'' by Minamoto no Morofusa is cited. After Fuyutsugu’s death, the Tōkyō Residence was divided into the eastern Kazan’in and the western Koichijō Residence. The same work records the following account told by the then master of the Koichijō Residence, Fujiwara no Morishige:
The Koichijō Residence had been purchased by Fujiwara no Uchinaro for his son Fuyutsugu because, when Fuyutsugu was still an Inner Palace Guard, the Munakata deity called out to him from the void while he was on his way to court, delivering an oracle that if he asked his father to buy the Koichijō Residence, lived there, and enshrined the Munakata deity beside him, the deity would protect his descendants for generations.
It appears that Ama-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami was also enshrined at the northeastern corner of the residence, though its origin is unknown.
The Tōkyō Residence was the birthplace of Emperor Seiwa in Kashō 3 (850) (his mother was Akiko, a granddaughter of Fuyutsugu), and for this reason the shrine came to be revered as his birth deity and tutelary deity. The three Munakata deities were granted the rank of Senior Second Rank in Jōgan 1 (859), later promoted to Junior First Rank, and in Jōgan 7 (865) Ama-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami, also a residence shrine, was granted Junior Third Rank. In the same year, shields, halberds, and saddles were especially dedicated to the shrine, though it was not listed in the ''Engishiki Shrine Register''. Later, during the time of Fujiwara no Tokihira, Ukanomitama-no-Kami was enshrined together. In Tenshō 1 (1131), when Fujiwara no Iezane inherited the Kazan’in (by then known as Kazan’in after having served as the imperial residence of Emperor Kazan) from Fujiwara no Morozane and established the Kazan’in family, Ama-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami was also enshrined together as the family’s guardian deity. The shrine was first listed as an official shrine in Kenji 1 (1275).
The shrine was destroyed by fire in the warfare of the Ōnin War, but was later rebuilt. As the surrounding area developed into a district of court nobles’ residences, the shrine remained at its location even after the Kazan’in family relocated. With Emperor Meiji’s transfer of the capital to Tokyo, the shrine came to be located within the Imperial Garden, and in Meiji 8 (1875) it was designated a prefectural shrine. After World War II, it became affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines.
=== Divine ranks ===
The three Munakata deities are recorded as having been granted Junior Second Rank with Eighth Order of Merit on the 30th day of the second month of Jōgan 1, promoted to Senior Second Rank the same day, and further promoted to Junior First Rank on October 11 of Jōgan 6 (864), according to the ''Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku''. In Kenji 1, the shrine was designated to receive offerings at the four annual imperial rites (the Kinensai, Tsukinamisai, and Niinamesai). The ''Ōkagami'' and ''Teiō Hennenk i'' also transmit a tale that Fujiwara no Yoshifusa, son of Fuyutsugu, was in constant conversation with the Munakata deity, and that, feeling apologetic that the deity’s rank was lower than his own, he arranged for the divine rank to be raised.
Ama-no-Ishido-Ake-no-Kami was promoted from no rank to Junior Third Rank on March 21 of Jōgan 7.
== Ritual administration ==
From the time the Kazan’in family inherited the estate until the Meiji period, members of that family served as bettō (administrators) and conducted the shrine’s rites.
== Shrine buildings ==
The main hall is a one-bay nagare-zukuri structure with cypress bark roofing. It was rebuilt in the Ansei era of the Edo period (mid-19th century).
== Sub-shrines ==
* **Hanei Inari Shrine** – Enshrines the Myōbu Inari deity. The ''Kazan’in Family Chronicle'' records that Fujiwara no Mototsune, adoptive son of Yoshifusa, enshrined it as his guardian deity. The ''Tsuchiyuki'' relates that when Mototsune was still of low rank, he rescued a fox being beaten by children; the fox later appeared in a dream and vowed to ward off calamities if given a place to dwell, and thus was assigned the present site as an attendant of the Munakata deity. One-bay nagare-zukuri with cypress bark roofing.
* **Shōshōi Shrine** – Enshrines Kushinadahime-no-Kami. It is said to have been relocated from the former temporary shrine of Yasaka Shrine between the neighborhoods of Shōshōi and Shōshōi Otabi. On July 24, during the Gion Festival’s later procession, priests from Yasaka Shrine still visit to offer sacred food and report the festival’s observance. Structure: nagare-mise-dana-zukuri with cypress bark roofing.
* **Kotohira Shrine** – Enshrines Ōmononushi-no-Kami and Emperor Sutoku. It was founded on October 10, Bunka 3 (1806), when Kyōgoku Takahiro, lord of the Marugame Domain in Sanuki Province, invited the deity of Kotohira Shrine. Structure: Kasuga-zukuri with cypress bark roofing.
* **Kazan Inari Shrine** – Located beneath a great camphor tree south of the precinct, enshrining Ukanomitama-no-Kami. It is said to have been revered as the guardian deity of the Kazan’in family. One-bay nagare-zukuri with cypress bark roofing. The camphor tree is said to be about 600 years old (as of 2010) and the oldest in the Imperial Garden.
* **Kyoto Tourism Shrine** – Enshrines Sarutahiko Ōkami. Founded on November 1, Shōwa 44 (1969) at the initiative of tourism operators to pray for visitors’ safety and the prosperity of the industry, inviting Sarutahiko as a guide deity. One-bay nagare-zukuri with copper plate roofing.
== Precincts ==
* **Former Sakon no Sakura** – Transplanted in Shōwa 11 (1936) when the Left Cherry Tree before the Shishinden of the Kyoto Imperial Palace was replanted.
